video_title: Consumers Feel Awful But Keep Spending with Michelle Meyer, Mastercard's Chief Economist
transcript: A very warm welcome to the risk reversal podcast. You know it's me that is Guyadami. Today I'm joined by Michelle Meyer. She's the chief economist at Mastercard. I thought we've had her on twice. Turns out only once. Very memorable. And if you think about the seat that she occupies, very timely as believe it or not, we head into the holiday shopping season. Hello Michelle. >> Thanks for having me back. >> It's always great. No, honestly, it's great to have you. I know you've been on Liz Thomas's podcast. I know you've been on CNBC and it's great to have you on ours. And you know, let's start with I think the obvious elephant in the room and that's interest rates which have been heading higher in a pretty meaningful way. And you know, like it or not, in the seat that you sit in in terms of consumerf facing, interest rates have a big big influence, a big impact on what goes on. >> Of course. Yeah. I mean impacts borrowing costs and borrowing costs are going to impact corporates are going to impact consumers. Um when you think about the direct link to consumers oftentimes you think about the housing market which for a potential new buyer or somebody who has an adjustable rate mortgage they're going to be much more sensitive to the everyday fluctuations of interest rates. And with a 30-year fixed rate mortgage now above 7% it's getting you know that much more expensive and affordability was already stretched to begin with. That said, for those that are not actively looking to buy a new home, for those that are sitting in a fixed rate mortgage at COVID levels 2 and a half, 3%, they're not necessarily experiencing that fluctuation the same way. And instead, they're seeing an equity market that is very supportive. If they have money in a checking account or money market or fixed income, they're obviously getting a better return now. So the level of interest rates is going to transmit very differently depending on the current state of that household. >> Yeah, no doubt about it. And you know, we play this game on fast money. If you had told me certain things six months ago and asked me to sort of gauge where things would be today, I would have made so many mistakes that would make your head spin. And you know, I would have thought the sensitivity around rates to the consumer, especially given the term that everybody loves to use, this K-shaped economy, would have been significant. But I don't think we're necessarily seeing it because, you know, there's still this strong consumer spending that we're seeing. So, help me to sort of wrap my head around that. I >> think consumers are driven by a variety of inputs. Interest rates is one. Again, if you are actively borrowing money in some capacity, you will feel it there. But the primary driver for consumer spending is the labor market. And we have seen an healthy labor market conditions, an unemployment rate hovering just above 4%. Faster churn now in the workforce, a broadening of job creation across different sectors, including into the goods economy. You have construction jobs that are picking up, not because of residential, but because of all the infrastructure that's being built in the economy to support the capex, the AI investment. Manufacturing, we're seeing job creation there as well. Well, you've seen the ISM surveys in expansionary territory in the last few months of job growth there as well. So, a healthy labor market is the most critical factor for consumers. And then you add on that the balance sheet which has looked very healthy given how much expansion there has been in terms of net worth over the last several years now. >> So, the consumers I say on fast money, I've been saying it for a long time because I've learned it the hard way that never underestimate the US consumers want to spend. It's should they be spending and if I'm listening you correctly there's an aspect of yeah you know what they should be spending because they're not in as bad a place as somebody like Gyodami thinks they might be. >> On aggregate the consumer is supported. Now of course there's different stories within that and that's where I think it gets complicated because not every household is seeing and feeling the economy the same way. But if you look at the total numbers, it is a consumer that is supported and that's why it translates to such healthy spending. As you mentioned, we're looking ahead to the holiday shopping season. We released our forecast last year, last week, and we're it felt like last year, last week, and we're looking for 5.5% year-over-year growth in holiday spend this year. That's the strongest in four years. Now, real quick, I mean, that is excluding auto and gas, which is a which, you know, but that's important to bring up because people would say, well, wait a second, guy. You know, think about what's going on in G, but you you back that out and you still have a pretty robust growth here. >> Yeah. So, Guy, that's absolutely important to underscore, which is not just, okay, well, yes, we know gas prices are up. People are spending nearly, you know, 15 20% year-over-year gains in at at the pump because of higher prices. That's not what's that's not what we're measuring here. We're taking a measure of holiday sales, which is retail sales taking out autos and and gas and a better representation of underlying spending as a result of the holidays. There's inflationary pressures there as well. So, we estimate about half of the gain in retail spend is due to inflation, but that means the other half is due to real volumes. That's due to real activity. That's a healthy breakdown. By the way, we'll put Michelle's report if with her permission in the show notes because I think it's important for people to read and it's certainly look I mean think about where you sit. I don't have to tell you but it's important for the audience to understand. I mean you're at the apex of everything. I mean think about where Mastercard is and what you have the ability to see. So before we get some of the other things just speak to to the extent that you can speak to the type of data that you have access to. >> Absolutely. I mean we have the pulse of the economy through the lens of the consumer truly. So we can we can look at aggregated anatomized um insights and data through our rails. So how consumers are spending on different types of segments in the economy in the sense of the breakdown of their their their their shopping basket. Right? So we can look at sector level data by MCC codes. We can look at how that varies across the globe, across the US, across zip codes. So you can get super granular to see how the economy is evolving, how the consumer is spending at different locations and on different sectors, which is so important going back to your initial point, which is sometimes it doesn't feel like it's all one story. Well, it's not. It's definitely not one story. We're seeing lots of different narratives that all aggregate up into this consumer spending trajectory which at the moment is strong. >> Let me ask you a question. I don't know if there's an answer to it, but you look at the University of Michigan consumer sentiment consumer sentiment in general has not been good and and it's you can probably explain it. Michigan specifically because that is an inflation sort of weighted survey I guess but it's pretty clear that people feel one way but yet they act an entirely different way through the lens of what you just gave us in terms of some of the numbers. Does that makes is that is there historic in terms of that or is that make sense to you? does not make a lot of sense to me. >> I think there's a question of the the way the survey questions are asked, I think, is a is a is something to look at. I think in general, we have to be really mindful when we consider surveys, especially long histories, because the survey response rates can change. Is it truly representative of the population that we're trying to survey? Because we know there's always sample concerns. So, take that with a grain of salt. That said, there's, you know, historically these surveys were helpful and trending with overall spending up until right after the pandemic when we started to see this real disconnect and spending outpac what would be implied from the sentiment surveys. And guy, you mentioned part of that is because of inflation that inflation is one of the reasons that could explain a gap. When inflation's high, you have more nominal spending, but consumers might not feel great about that. So, that might hurt sentiment. That was a big part of the story in 2022 when he started to see the gap evolve. But what's important is even once inflation over the next few years started to come back in back closer to core, the gap never really resolved itself. So I think there's more there that's probably driving this disconnect or potentially lingering concern amongst the survey responses. And I and I think part of it is, and you know this better than most, but the cumulative effect of inflation is is important. And you know, you'll have pundits and politicians come out and say inflation is going lower. That's not really what's happening. It's just going up less fast, which sounds somewhat nuanced, but it's not. And I think part of this is that, you know, the this prolonged persistent inflation is finally weighing on at least the psyche of people. Well, I think there's a difference between the price level versus the rate of change of prices. So, as economists, as market participants, we're focused on inflation, which is the rate of change of prices. But after a period of of a of a big shock up in prices and if it doesn't come back down, which it hasn't, that starts to feel like this like cumulative inflation shock because the level of prices are higher. The challenge with looking at it just that way is that you can't just think about the price of goods and services in isolation. You have to think about that level relative to wages, relative to asset prices, relative to all other types of prices, commodities, etc. that are out there. And and that's where I think it becomes a lot more quote unquote acceptable, at least from the point of an economist, because we've seen wages also inflate. We've seen asset prices inflate tremendously, right? When you think about how much they're up over the last few years. So the the inflation numbers we're looking at CPI or core PCE, which is the the Fed's preferred gauge, looks somewhat reasonable in the context of the broader economy. >> Excellent point by you. Clearly, I did not expect anything, but but you know, the if there's a slight push back, I think, and you probably have the data in front of you. I think over the last three months or so that wage growth has sort of now sort of gone the wrong way in terms of inflation. Now maybe that's just I don't know you know sometimes you just get some quirks in the numbers or so but my question to you is if in fact that is true which I think it is when does that become a trend that's concerning? So right now wages are hovering very close to headline inflation. The extent to which energy prices continue to rise, you're absolutely right, that can start to impair wages and you can see negative real wages, but we're like right on that line at the moment. I think it's the persistence of it that will really matter. So watch energy prices pay close attention to diesel prices as well particularly because there's a threat that diesel prices could pass into underlying goods inflation if input costs become too high for retailers for wholesalers etc. But right now we're kind of at very close to an equilibrium and in an environment where the labor market is still very tight it should remain that way. seems like, you know, and and to your point, we're right there sort of on the precipice, and that's when it starts to get into people's mind when they start realizing, well, wait a second, my dollar doesn't go as far as it did this time last year. So, it's it's something to watch for sure, and we'll see. Now, the term K-shaped economy gets thrown around. The reality is whether or not you're exercised by it, it's a real thing. And if you listen, if you read these earnings calls, I mean, there's something clearly going on in terms of the high income versus the middle to lower income spending that continues to widen. That chasm continues to grow. Is that a fair assessment? >> So, here's the way that I would think about it is that the balance sheet effects, the health of the household balance sheet disproportionately is going to support those that have exposure to it, which is the upper income household. So it is the case that spending is growing faster amongst that cohort. But it is not the case that spending is contracting for the lower income. So we are still there's still evidence very clear evidence I think that spending is increasing across all the income groups. But it may be the case naturally that the upper income that is experiencing these positive wealth effects is just seeing faster spending growth. I've gone about 15 minutes and I haven't mentioned artificial intelligence, but I will now because my instincts suggests that the consumer is starting to get his or her arms around what it means for their ability to to figure out uh the retail market. And I don't know what it means for this holiday spending. It might mean people wait longer. I I don't know what's going to happen, but AI is going to start to play a meaningful role, I think, in the seat that you occupy. Is that fair? That is so accurate and actually we've started exploring this. So we have some answers to your questions in terms of how AI can impact the holiday season and we have a unique lens to look at this because we have the ability to understand the cohort of consumers that have AI subscriptions. So AI users and you can look at how spending evolves and how consumers behave versus a cohort that don't have AI subscriptions that aren't as engaged with AI tools. And it's fascinating. There's two observations so far and we'll see how this plays out in the holiday season. But the first observation is that AI power users go to a wider number of merchants to spend. So there's greater dispersion of purchasing power across multiple merchants. Um, and that really shows up in a handful of categories. The number one is beauty services. We see it in specialty food stores. We see it in restaurants and florists where there's an ability to search, where there's ability to be like super specialized and really pointed. I think it's it's it's clear that uh AI users are going to explore many many many more merchants than somebody who's not an AI user. You don't see the same dispersion or differential when you look at things like video game stores or home improvement or grocery stores where you there's a similar um variety of merchants that are that are visited by AI and non AI users. So that's the first observation. The second one is around the timing of the holiday season. We see evidence that there's an earlier engagement in the holiday season for AI users, whereas the non-A users will have a greater share of their spending at the very end of the season. >> It is a fascinating it's going to be a fascinating thing to watch if it if it lends to if it leads itself to the ability for a dollar to go farther for the consumer, right? if they've figured out how to sort of tap into this thing and and how that changes historic norms and historic data. Anyway, that's just something to throw out there. >> My my next question to you is again, Mastercard is at the pinnacle of all this in terms of seeing what you're what you have the ability to see. What is the most important and I'm not asking you to play stock market because that's not fair but in terms of metrics that you provide in these reports like what is the one thing that when the reports come out the your eyes go to this first is it trans total transactions transaction what is that metric >> well I would can talk to what we produce at the economics institute leveraging all of the information I think our spending pulse metric is probably one of the best in terms of understanding underlying spend. So it's an aggregation of spending that's kind of panled up and representative of the broader population. So it's a really nice highfrequency segmented uh by different types of um MCC's or you know different types of sectors in the economy. So you can really see how the consumer basket is shifting. You can see an overall growth rates and it's and its high frequency. Another metric that I think is really helpful and useful is to be able to break down spending between the number of transactions versus the average transaction value. So again, you can get an idea of how much is kind of real volume versus potentially pricing. >> It is if you know I love the reports. I think the last time Mastercard reports I think the end of July. I think you're due to report in October. And I just love looking at the numbers because you you can glean so much from all those different things. And again, not taking credit into consideration is it's just transaction processing. It really you can really learn a lot about what's going on, which is why this is a perfect time to have you. and I said we're going to put your holiday sort of forecast in, but you're also going to come out with a, if you have not already, and I apologize, 2027 outlook is coming to a theater near you. So, let's talk about that. >> Well, we're going to release our outlook uh early December. So, we'll we'll I'll be back then to talk in a lot more detail. But, as we look ahead into 27, we do see a global economy that is continuing to expand. So we see further growth particularly in the US. I think the big thing to look at and focus on is how much more investment we may see in the economy that can power overall growth because if you look at the decomposition of of of of GDP this year certainly capex and investment has has done a lot in terms of driving spend and it is driving GDP in addition to spending. So a big question I think for 27 is how much more investment will we see across the globe particularly related to the adoption of AI. >> Yeah. And one of the t one of the headlines I think is probably going to be you know never never doubt the US consumer and that's something I said earlier in our conversation you know never underestimate the US consumers want to spend. The question I think you have to continually look at is should they be spending which leads us back quickly to the labor market and the Fed made it pretty clear in October I guess at Jackson Hole that what they were really going to be focused on now inflation is the problem right I mean the labor market seemingly is okay for them and inflation is problem what we can debate whether or not that's correct but you have to be looking at the labor market very closely I would say there is there anything that you see that gives you tremendous optimism or conversely is there anything that you see that's sort of giving you pause here? >> So I would say there's two things that are interesting to look at in addition to the headline numbers. One is the breadth of job creation. So is it the case that we're seeing broader job growth across sectors? And I think the answer is yes. Right now that is happening where if you look at the diffusion of jobs. The second one is the turnover of the of the labor market and and so you can look at things like the jolts rates, but you can also look at just the the likelihood of finding a job once you've been unemployed. And for that, the ratio of job openings to unemployed is helpful. And we have seen an increase in the number of job openings for those that are looking. It's just above one. So that does imply that the extent to which there is a turnover of the workforce if somebody is unemployed hopefully presumably they're not sitting out of work as long which helps to support their wage growth and therefore their spending power. So trying to understand the churn and the and the breath of job creation I think is is very important. >> Yeah. And and I'm glad you brought that up because I and you know again I think much better than I do, but at one point over the last five or six years, I think there were approximately 13 and a half million job openings for about a little less than 7 million people looking. And I'm not the brightest person, but I can do that math. It was almost 2 to one, which speaks >> that was 2022, 2023. Yeah, >> look at me, right? I was pretty I think my numbers are pretty close, right? >> I don't know offhand, but that sounds that sounds. And I only bring it up because you know if you think about just again it's economics. If you have more job openings than people looking I mean it's going to sort of favor the people looking for the job and that lends itself to wage growth. And if it's yes, >> you know I don't know what I guess my question is at what point is that is it we're one to one nowish as you just said like where does this sort of get dicey >> the wrong way >> in either direction is the wrong equilibrium. I think to your point, if it goes too much back to where we were a few years ago when we had a red-hot labor market, then the you start to see a gap between wages for those that have quit and found a new job where the wage growth would be higher than job stayers. So, job switchers start to outpace the wage growth of job stayers. And that shows a labor market that's probably too hot and therefore would would be consistent with a Federal Reserve that needs to start hiking and prevent a wage price spiral from developing. But the other side of it is also obviously very concerning. If you start to have a lot of people out there looking for jobs and the jobs aren't available, then it's an indication that something's happening in corporate America where companies are no longer looking to expand their workforce or they're looking to shrink or cut costs or there's something else that's brewing that could be problematic when we think about the health of the economy. So either direction, you know, you want if you move too much in in either way, it's a point of concern. So where we are now is like is really optimal, >> right? Sweet spot. No. And I just brought it up because I mean all these things that I I know you watch because you're that's that's your role, but I don't think a lot of people Yeah, that's what you do. A lot of people don't really look at it that granularly given your seat, do you sort of take a gander at some of the bigname retailers or consumerf facing stocks to try to sort of figure out if your thesis or what you're seeing makes sense or if there's something a skew? I mean, we take all information. So, we're looking at obviously the broader economic data. We're looking at what we see from consumer spending. We're looking at financial market indicators. There's no data that we don't like that we don't look at. But I think the reality is is that, you know, in you have to kind of take out the individual story from the bigger picture. And as economists, we're looking at the macro trends. We're looking at the broader spending trends. And as I mentioned, it doesn't all feel and look the same depending on how you participate in the economy. And it hasn't for the last several years. If you go back to the COVID period when we were first in COVID, it was the experience economy was in trouble and the goods economy was booming. You couldn't get a couch. You could not buy a new piece of furniture because there was so much demand and challenged inventories. Um, and that ex exert upper pressure on pricing. And then once the reopening happened, it reversed and the experience economy started to boom. I mean, we've had these cycles and this like >> different stages I suppose you can say of the economy and growth for different sectors and that I think does complicate the story quite a lot. >> Yeah, it again there's so I again I'll use a term that I don't really like using but you have to the crosscurrens in your world are significant, right? I mean there there's enough for everybody out there. If you want to sort of take the bare thesis of things, there's a there's a treasure trove of data that supports that. And the flip side, if you want to be optimistic about things, there's an equal amount of data that supports it. And it's hard to sort of wrap your head around it. And and it it's manifesting itself in these individual names. I mean, there's certain retail stocks that if you look at, you think things have never been better. And the other side of the coin is like what's really going on? So that's why it's so important to have >> there's a lot of consumer choice. I do think consumers have had a lot of power frankly in the last few years because they have so much more information. They are being very very mindful of how they're using their purchasing power to find and optimize value. So it's not the case that you know consumers just going to go to the the their shopping center down the road and take whatever price they see in a store. they're going to they have the ability to to to to shop to look to find an alternative that might be overseas that's going to be able to get here. So the barriers to entry for small businesses are lower. There's a lot more innovation in the retail space and I think that changes the equation. >> Yeah, 100%. And that goes back to the AI conversation we had and how that's going to absolutely change the equation which is why you have to when your report comes out in the beginning of December, I hope you'll join us. Um, we're going to put the holiday uh piece that you wrote, put it in our show notes. And before you leave, and again, obviously, thank you for your time. Michelle shared with us prior to us uh taping this that she is sporting some risk reversal swag. I don't know if you have it in front of you, but if you can show it to >> So, not only is she a participant, but she is a user of the brand. Michelle Meyer, chief economist at Mascard, thank you so much for joining us. >> You got it. Thank you for having me. I'll talk to you in early December for Outlook.
